details:
**Mansa Musa's hajj**
Mansa Musa I, Mali's most famous ruler, made a pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 with a huge caravan of attendants and camels carrying gold. He gave away and spent so much gold, especially in Cairo, that its value fell in Egypt for years. Legend says he built a mosque every Friday along the way, and this hajj is the giveaway in almost every Mali question.

**Sundiata Keita**
The Mandinka founder of the Mali Empire in the 13th century. According to oral tradition he was the son of the hunchbacked Sogolon and was born unable to walk, but he overcame this, returned from exile, and united the Mandinka against the Sosso. He set his capital at Niani, and the empire grew out of the small Mandinka state of Kangaba.

**Battle of Kirina and Sumanguru**
The battle (c. 1235) in which Sundiata defeated Sumanguru (Soumaoro) Kanté, the sorcerer-king of the Sosso. Legend says Sundiata destroyed Sumanguru's magic by hitting him with an arrow tipped with the spur of a white rooster. The victory founded the empire.

**Sankore University and Timbuktu**
Timbuktu, a trading city on the Niger River, became Mali's great center of Islamic learning. Its Sankore mosque, built of mud brick, grew into the madrasa known as the University of Sankore, traditionally credited to Mansa Musa. The later scholar Ahmad Baba was associated with it.

**Gbara (Great Assembly)**
Mali's deliberative assembly, which checked the power of the mansa (emperor). It included representatives of the leading clans and groups, among them the military "Carriers of Quivers" and the Dyula merchants.

**Kouroukan Fouga**
The founding charter or "constitution" of the Mali Empire, traditionally proclaimed by Sundiata after the Battle of Kirina at Kangaba. It contained forty-four edicts, organized society into clans and castes, and set up the Gbara.

**"Carriers of Quivers"**
The sixteen noble clans responsible for Mali's military forces, said to descend from Sundiata's companions. They were drawn from the free horon class and formed a voting bloc in the Gbara.

**Griots and the Epic of Sundiata**
Griots are hereditary Mandinka storytellers, musicians, and keepers of oral history. They preserved the Epic of Sundiata, the oral epic that tells of Sundiata's childhood, exile, and victory over Sumanguru.

**Al-Sahili and the Djinguereber Mosque**
Abu Ishaq al-Sahili was an Andalusian poet and architect who returned with Mansa Musa from his hajj. He is credited with designing the Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu and a royal audience chamber that the historian Ibn Khaldun praised as an "admirable monument." Islamist militants damaged Timbuktu's shrines in 2012.

**Twelve Doors**
The name for the core possessions and allied territories that made up the Mali Empire, including lands such as Siby and the Kaniaga region taken from the Sosso.

**Mansa (title)**
The title of Mali's emperors, roughly meaning "king of kings." Holders included the founder Sundiata, Mansa Musa, and Sakura, a former slave who seized the throne in the late 13th century.

**Atlantic expeditions of Abu Bakr II**
The Arab writer al-Umari records Mansa Musa's account that his predecessor sent a fleet of ships to explore the Atlantic, none of which returned except one whose captain reported a river with a powerful current. The ruler then set out with an even larger fleet and never came back, and Musa took the throne.

**Catalan Atlas**
A 1375 map from Majorca that shows Mansa Musa enthroned in West Africa, wearing a crown and holding a gold nugget and a scepter. It reflects how famous Mali's wealth had become in Europe.

**Ibn Battuta and Taghaza**
The Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta visited Mali in 1352–1353 under Mansa Suleyman and described its court and its salt-mining town of Taghaza, a key source of the salt traded for gold across the Sahara.

**Decline and the Songhai Empire**
Mali weakened in the 15th century as Gao rebelled, Tuareg raiders took Timbuktu, and Bamana and other groups attacked. The Songhai Empire, centered at Gao, replaced it as the dominant power of West Africa.
